desc:
You may change the value stored in any node of a binary tree to any integer (negative values and values above 10,000 are allowed), but you may not change the shape of the tree. A tree is a valid binary search tree when for every node all values in its left subtree are strictly smaller than the node's value and all values in its right subtree are strictly larger.

Return the minimum number of nodes whose value has to be changed so that the tree becomes a valid BST. If it already is one, the answer is 0.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [3, 1, 2] (root 3, left child 1, right child 2) the answer is 1: change the 2 to 4. For tree = [2, 2, 2] the answer is 2, because a BST has distinct values and at most one of the 2s can stay. For tree = [4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7] the answer is 0.
constraints: Every tree array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: A tree is a strict BST exactly when its inorder sequence is strictly increasing, so only the inorder sequence matters, not the shape. The problem becomes: change the fewest entries of an array so that it is strictly increasing.

Choose a set of entries to keep. Between two kept entries at positions i < j there must be room for j - i - 1 distinct integers, which means a[j] - a[i] ≥ j - i. Entries before the first and after the last kept one have unlimited room because any integer is allowed.

The condition a[j] - j ≥ a[i] - i says that the numbers b[i] = a[i] - i of the kept entries form a non-decreasing subsequence. Maximise its length (longest non-decreasing subsequence with binary search, O(n log n)); the answer is n minus that length.
editorial: Reduce to an array. A binary tree is a strict BST if and only if its inorder traversal is strictly increasing, and the shape does not change, so the nodes keep their positions in the inorder order. Let a[0..n-1] be the inorder values. We want the largest set of positions that can keep their values; all others are changed (and changing a node is allowed to produce any integer, so changed nodes are never the bottleneck).

Kept positions i < j that are neighbours in the kept set need j - i - 1 distinct integers strictly between a[i] and a[j] for the changed nodes between them, which is possible exactly when a[j] - a[i] ≥ j - i, i.e. a[j] - j ≥ a[i] - i. Before the first kept and after the last kept position there is no limit. Checking neighbouring kept pairs is enough, since the condition is transitive.

So the kept positions form a non-decreasing subsequence of b[i] = a[i] - i. The longest non-decreasing subsequence is computed in O(n log n) with the patience-sorting array and bisect_right, and the answer is n minus its length. Producing the inorder sequence takes an iterative traversal in O(n). Note that equal inorder values give strictly decreasing b, so at most one of them can be kept.
